metadata.title: A Deep Reinforcement Learning Approach for Ramp Metering Based on Traffic Video Data
supplementary_materials: data used to support the results of this study are available from the corresponding author upon request

hyperparameters.name: State matrix dimension
hyperparameters.context: Dimension of the visual representation extracted from raw images to represent traffic states

hyperparameters.name: Replay buffer size B
hyperparameters.context: Size of the buffer that stores data prepared for training into the replay buffer

hyperparameters.name: Learning rate eta
hyperparameters.context: Step size used for updating weights in the Q-network by the Adam optimizer

hyperparameters.name: Batch size k
hyperparameters.context: Number of transitions uniformly sampled from the replay buffer to compute gradients

hyperparameters.name: Exploration rate epsilon
hyperparameters.context: Probability of taking a random action to explore unknown policies

hyperparameters.name: Freeze interval F
hyperparameters.context: Frequency at which target network parameters are updated by copying the Q-network weights

hyperparameters.name: Decision step size L
hyperparameters.context: Fixed time interval at which the ramp meter takes actions to determine signal phases

hyperparameters.name: Loss weight lambda
hyperparameters.context: Weight applied to the multitask learning prediction loss function

metadata.hardware_requirements: computing server with NVIDIA Quadro K620 GPU and Intel Xeon CPU E5-1650 (3.6 GHz, 6 cores)

nodes_source.node_name: Qingdao and Huangdao real-world traffic data
nodes_source.source_quote: A series of simulation experiments based on real-world traffic data are conducted to evaluate the proposed approach.
nodes_source.description: Empirical traffic volume and behavioral data from a freeway connecting Qingdao and Huangdao in Shandong, China, used to calibrate simulation parameters in the SUMO microscopic traffic simulator.
nodes_source.reproducibility_rationale: The paper explicitly states in the Data Availability section that data are available from the corresponding author upon request.

nodes_process.source_quote: Vehicle locations are extracted from the traffic video frames and are reformed as position matrices.
nodes_process.description: Vehicles are represented by a location point (xi, yi) in raw images. A control area of size X by Y is mapped to a position matrix mt, where pixels with vehicles are assigned constant UV.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=4, generic tool stated, all params in Table 1.

nodes_process.source_quote: we stack the matrices of consecutive N time steps to represent the state st
nodes_process.description: N consecutive matrices are stacked to represent vehicle dynamics. Down-sampling is used to reduce input dimensions while maintaining vehicle position information.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=3, stacking logic specified but down-sampling factor unclear.

nodes_process.source_quote: The algorithm for training the ramp metering policy is presented in Algorithm 1.
nodes_process.description: Train a multitask DRL agent with experience replay and a target network using Adam. Losses L1 (DQN) and L2 (speed/queue prediction) are combined with weight lambda. Uses epsilon-greedy exploration.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=4, algorithm and architecture (Figure 7) detailed, but gamma omitted in Table 1.

nodes_process.source_quote: The proposed method is evaluated in SUMO, an open-source microscopic traffic simulator
nodes_process.description: The trained policy is evaluated against No-Control and PI-ALINEA baselines in 20 simulation experiments of a real-world freeway merge in Shandong, China.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=4, simulation environment and scenario (Figure 5) fully specified.

nodes_sink.source_quote: The training process, presented in Figure 8, can be finished in less than 24 hours on a computing server with NVIDIA Quadro K620 GPU.
nodes_sink.description: Convergence curves showing (a) episode reward and (b) mean travel time (s) across 1 million training frames.
nodes_sink.reproducibility_rationale: Hardware and hyperparameters defined; specific training trace requires seed replication.

nodes_sink.source_quote: Overall, the proposed DRL method results in shorter travel times with narrower travel time ranges than that of the fine-tuned PI-ALINEA method.
nodes_sink.description: Mainline travel times (min) for three scenarios (No control, PI-ALINEA, Deep RL) over time intervals from 8:00 to 9:00.
nodes_sink.reproducibility_rationale: Comparison based on SUMO simulation results with specified calibrated behavior parameters.

nodes_sink.source_quote: Table 2 presents mean vehicle travel times in 20 simulation experiments. ... DRL method consistently results in a shorter travel time than that of the no-control scenario.
nodes_sink.description: Numerical mean travel times (s) and percentage improvements for 20 independent simulation experiments under three control scenarios.
nodes_sink.reproducibility_rationale: Explicit trial counts and comparative values provided; logically derivable from aggregate metrics.

nodes_sink.source_quote: Figure 10 presents the temporal-spatial distribution of the mean speeds along the mainline. ... better performance of the proposed method.
nodes_sink.description: Temporal-spatial speed heatmaps comparing freeway segments (distance 0-4000m) and time (8:00-9:00) for (a) no-control, (b) PI-ALINEA, and (c) DRL.
nodes_sink.reproducibility_rationale: Heatmap resolution not precisely specified; outcomes plausibly follow from simulation trajectories.

nodes_sink.source_quote: Nevertheless, the queues produced by the proposed method are shorter than those produced by the PI-ALINEA method.
nodes_sink.description: Time-series comparison of on-ramp queue length distributions (Q1, Q2, Q3) for No control, PI-ALINEA, and Deep RL scenarios.
nodes_sink.reproducibility_rationale: Standard SUMO queue metrics; scenario results are clearly distinguished and supported by Tab 2.

nodes_sink.source_quote: queue length generally increases with the red ratio. However ... the queues produced by the DRL method are shorter.
nodes_sink.description: Scatter plot and linear regression showing the relationship between queue length and signal red ratio for two metering methods.
nodes_sink.reproducibility_rationale: Clear statistical visualization of control efficiency using outputs from the 20 simulation trials.

nodes_sink.source_quote: queue length and the occupancy are highly correlated when the PI-ALINEA method is adopted. ... the correlation is relatively low when the DRL method is implemented.
nodes_sink.description: Correlation comparison (rho=0.93 vs rho=0.50) between mainline occupancy and on-ramp queue length for PI-ALINEA and Deep RL.
nodes_sink.reproducibility_rationale: Directly summarizes simulation observations; correlation coefficients explicitly stated.

nodes_sink.source_quote: During the peak period between 8:10-8:35, the flows resulting from the DRL method are higher and more stable.
nodes_sink.description: Box plots of downstream traffic volume (veh/h) sampled across time intervals for No control, PI-ALINEA, and Deep RL scenarios.
nodes_sink.reproducibility_rationale: Aggregates flow data from simulations; 5-minute sampling interval is evident but not explicit.

nodes_sink.source_quote: information from other subareas such as subarea 3 and 4 also influences the control performance obviously.
nodes_sink.description: Sensitivity analysis box plot showing mean travel time variations when video input from specific road subareas is perturbed or removed.
nodes_sink.reproducibility_rationale: Procedure for input perturbation specified via subareas defined in Fig 15; outcomes logically feasible.
